stories.title: Fighting Neighbours? Singapore Now Has a Peacemaker for That!
stories.headline_kid: From next week, neighbours who keep quarrelling can be told to sit down and talk it out — by law!
summary: Do you know any neighbours who argue about noise, smells, or pets? In Tampines, officers have been trying out a special way to help neighbours solve their fights peacefully. It worked so well that from 1 September, this scheme will be used all over Singapore.

Here's how it works: if two neighbours cannot stop quarrelling on their own, the authorities can now send them a 'mediation direction'. This is like being called to the principal's office, except instead of getting punished, the neighbours sit with a helper called a mediator who guides them to talk calmly and find a fair solution.

The big change is that neighbours cannot simply ignore the invitation anymore — they can be legally required to turn up. This matters a lot in Singapore because most of us live close together in HDB flats, where sounds and smells travel easily between homes.
The goal is to stop small arguments from turning into big, nasty fights that end up in court. Officials hope this will make HDB estates calmer and friendlier places to live.

lenses.me: If your family ever has a noisy or smelly neighbour, there is now a proper, fair way to solve the problem instead of shouting matches.
lenses.family: Parents living in flats can ask for help through this scheme if disagreements with neighbours don't go away on their own.
lenses.friends: Classmates all over Singapore, not just in Tampines, now benefit from this dispute-solving system.
lenses.nation: It shows how Singapore tests new ideas in one area first, then rolls them out nationwide if they work well.
lenses.world: Other crowded cities facing similar neighbour conflicts might look at Singapore's idea as an example to copy.

stories.title: Haze Turns Worse in Malaysia as Dry Season Bites
stories.headline_kid: Smoke from forest fires in Indonesia is making the sky hazy and the air unhealthy in parts of Malaysia — and it could reach us too.
summary: Every year around this time, Singapore's neighbours worry about haze. This year, the dry season is making things worse, and fires burning in Kalimantan and Sumatra in Indonesia are sending thick smoke drifting across the region.

In Malaysia, the smoke has become so thick that air quality in parts of Sarawak and the Klang Valley (the area around Kuala Lumpur) has reached 'unhealthy' levels. Photos even show the tall Petronas Twin Towers almost disappearing into the smoky haze!

Haze happens when tiny bits of ash and smoke float in the air, making it hard to breathe and even harder to see far away. Doctors say breathing in hazy air for too long can cause coughing, sore throats, and trouble breathing, especially for children and the elderly.
Singapore has faced haze problems before too, so this is a good reminder to check the air quality app before playing outside, and to keep a mask ready just in case the haze drifts our way.

lenses.family: Families may need to keep windows closed and check the PSI (air quality) readings before outdoor outings.
lenses.friends: Outdoor school activities like sports day could be affected if the haze becomes bad here too.
lenses.nation: Singapore works closely with Malaysia and Indonesia to fight fires and reduce haze across the region.
lenses.world: This shows how pollution doesn't stay in one country — smoke from fires can travel and affect millions of people far away.

stories.title: A Wall of Mud and Water Swept Away Hundreds of Lives in the Himalayas
stories.headline_kid: A giant mudslide flood in Nepal and Tibet has killed over 400 people, and scientists say melting glaciers may be to blame.
summary: Imagine a huge wave of mud, rocks, ice, and water suddenly rushing down a valley for over 170km — that is what happened along the Bhote Koshi River, which flows between Nepal and Tibet (part of China). The flood struck with almost no warning three days ago.

So far, more than 400 people have died, and over 1,000 people are still missing. Rescue workers are digging through thick mud with heavy machines and sniffer dogs, searching for survivors and bodies. Sadly, a lake formed by the debris has started overflowing, which is so dangerous that rescuers had to pause their search near the worst-hit area.

Scientists believe this disaster may have been caused by a melting glacier. Glaciers are giant, slow-moving rivers of ice found on mountains. As our planet gets warmer, glaciers are melting faster, sometimes forming unstable lakes that can suddenly burst and send a 'tsunami of dirt' rushing downhill.

This tragedy is a reminder that a warming world can cause sudden, deadly disasters far from where we live. Singapore does not have glaciers, but many Singaporean trekkers and tourists visit Nepal every year, so this news hits close to home for some families.

lenses.me: It helps you understand that climate change isn't just about hot weather — it can also cause sudden disasters like this one.
lenses.family: If your family enjoys travelling or hiking, this is a reminder to always check weather and safety warnings before a trip.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can learn about glaciers and climate change together in geography lessons.
lenses.nation: Singapore, like many countries, may send help or donations to support disaster relief efforts in Nepal.
lenses.world: Scientists warn that as glaciers keep melting worldwide, more communities could face similar dangerous floods in future.

stories.title: Singapore to Get a Brand New 1,000-Seat Theatre by 2030
stories.headline_kid: A big new theatre is coming to Tanglin, giving Singapore's actors, dancers, and musicians a shiny new stage to shine on.
summary: Good news for anyone who loves plays, concerts, or dance shows — Singapore is getting a brand new theatre! It will be built at the site of the old Tanglin Shopping Centre and is expected to be ready by 2030.

This will be a purpose-built theatre with 1,000 seats, designed especially for big performances. 'Purpose-built' means it is made specifically for one job — in this case, hosting amazing shows — rather than being a building that was changed to fit a different use.

The theatre will be able to host large local and international productions, giving Singaporean artists a bigger, better stage to perform on. It also creates new job opportunities for people working behind the scenes, like lighting designers, sound engineers, and stage crew.
This project shows how Singapore keeps investing in the arts, hoping to become an even bigger hub for culture and entertainment in Asia.

lenses.me: If you enjoy drama, dance, or music, this could be a place you visit — or even perform in — one day!
lenses.family: Families will have a brand new venue to catch concerts, plays, or musicals together in future.
lenses.friends: Classmates who love the performing arts have another reason to dream big about being on stage.
lenses.nation: It strengthens Singapore's reputation as a country that supports and grows its arts and culture scene.
lenses.world: The theatre could attract famous international shows to Singapore, putting our tiny island on the world's cultural map.

stories.title: Walking Dinosaurs Are Coming to Singapore This December!
stories.headline_kid: Fifteen super-realistic robot dinosaurs will roam close enough to touch at Resorts World Sentosa this December!
summary: Ever wished you could see a real T-rex without it eating you? This December, you might get the next best thing! Japan's famous live show, Dinosaur Odyssey, is coming to Singapore for the very first time.

The show will take place at Resorts World Convention Centre from 3 to 6 December. It features 15 ultra-realistic dinosaurs that move, stomp, and roar as they wander around close to the audience — some might even come within arm's reach!

These dinosaurs are actually clever machines controlled by skilled puppeteers or technology, built to look and move just like the real creatures that lived millions of years ago. It is Dinosaur Odyssey's first big indoor show held outside Japan, which shows how popular and impressive the production has become.
For dinosaur fans, this could be an unforgettable school holiday outing — just don't forget to bring your camera (and maybe your bravery)!

lenses.nation: It shows Singapore attracting exciting international entertainment, boosting tourism and fun activities here.
lenses.world: Singapore becomes the first country outside Japan to host this large-scale show, showing our growing role as a regional entertainment hub.
